name: Bolasterone (Finaject)

angle.text: Bolasterone is a veterinary oral steroid from the Upjohn era that appears in steroid histories as a mass and strength compound. It now features mostly in anti-doping detection papers; its physique use rests on class effects.

summary: An obscure Upjohn-era veterinary oral steroid, now mostly a name in anti-doping detection papers.
note: WADA-banned; no human trials found.
currentQuick:
Bolasterone is an oral anabolic steroid made by Upjohn for veterinary use. It is banned in sport.
Very little has been published about it beyond detection methods, so there is no human evidence for appearance or muscle effects.
How it works: It is a methylated testosterone analog; the 17-methyl group lets it work when swallowed. Its anabolic-to-androgenic ratio is described as low to moderate.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data exist. Risks are inferred from other 17-alkylated oral steroids. It is prohibited by WADA and controlled in some countries such as Brazil.
deepLead:
Bolasterone, chemically 7-alpha,17-alpha-dimethyltestosterone, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid developed by the Upjohn Company for veterinary use. Its 17-alpha-methyl group improves oral bioavailability and its 7-alpha-methyl group is shared with its isomer calusterone .
It is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency and is listed as a controlled anabolic steroid in Brazil . Wikipedia notes an unreferenced claim that East German authorities obtained it for athletes through the state sports-medicine research institute .
Little published material covers bolasterone. Most of the scientific literature that mentions it concerns detection chemistry in doping control, not effects on people, and no clinical trials were found.

name: Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (Turinabol / Oral Turinabol)

angle.text: Turinabol is the oral steroid of East German doping fame, favored by bodybuilders for lean, dry muscle gains. Its history and detection science are well documented; it is untested as a treatment for appearance.

summary: The oral steroid of East German doping fame; well documented in history and detection science, untested as a treatment.
note: Banned in sport; controlled in the US, UK and Brazil.
currentQuick:
Oral-Turinabol was Jenapharm's oral steroid, made from metandienone with an added chlorine atom. It was used for decades in East Germany's state doping programme.
Its reputation among lifters comes from that history. No clinical trials test it for muscle or appearance.
How it works: It is an androgen-receptor agonist derived from metandienone. Its 17-methyl group allows oral use, and it is metabolised in the liver to metabolites that can be detected in urine for a long time.
Risks and caveats: Documented evidence is limited to case reports and general anabolic-steroid concerns, including a case report of a testicular tumour after high-dose use. It is banned in sport and controlled in several countries.
deepLead:
Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (CDMT, DHCMT), sold as Oral-Turinabol and nicknamed Tbol, is an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 4-chloro derivative of metandienone. It was the first original product of the East German pharmaceutical company Jenapharm, patented in 1961, introduced clinically in 1965 and discontinued in 1994 .
It is best known as the central drug in East Germany's state doping programme, which according to Wikipedia ran from about 1968 to 1989 and involved thousands of athletes . Long-lasting urinary metabolites identified in 2012 allowed retrospective re-testing of stored Olympic samples .
Published clinical research on Oral-Turinabol as a treatment is scarce. The literature consists largely of metabolism and detection studies, plus isolated case reports of harm.

name: Clostebol (4-chlorotestosterone)

angle.text: Clostebol is a chlorinated testosterone mostly known from skin creams and doping cases, and bodybuilders have discussed it for lean mass. Appearance trials do not exist; the muscle use is based on class effects and anecdote.

summary: A chlorinated testosterone mostly known from skin creams and doping cases, with no appearance trials.
note: WADA-banned; positives have sometimes been traced to contamination.
currentQuick:
Clostebol is a testosterone derivative with a chlorine atom added. It is sold in some countries as a topical wound-healing product and has been used as a steroid ester.
It shows up mainly in doping news. No studies test it for muscle or appearance.
How it works: It is an androgen-receptor agonist. The chlorine is said to stop conversion to DHT and oestrogen. Its anabolic effect is described as modest.
Risks and caveats: Risks are inferred from anabolic steroids in general; clostebol-specific human safety data for physique use are lacking. It is prohibited in sport and controlled in the US, Canada and Brazil.
deepLead:
Clostebol, also called 4-chlorotestosterone, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from testosterone by adding a chlorine atom at the 4-position. It is usually formulated as an ester such as clostebol acetate, caproate or propionate .
Its main legitimate uses are topical: clostebol acetate has been used in dermatological and ophthalmological products, and in some countries, including Italy, creams and sprays containing it are sold for skin wounds . It is prohibited at all times by the World Anti-Doping Agency and appears regularly in doping cases, some of them attributed to accidental transdermal contamination .
No clinical trials have tested clostebol for appearance or physique. The published literature on it is dominated by anti-doping analysis.

name: Danazol

angle.text: Danazol is a prescription steroid for endometriosis and angioedema that has been mentioned in bodybuilding forums for its weak androgenic effects. It is studied for medical conditions; an appearance use is untested.

summary: A prescription antigonadotropin steroid for endometriosis and angioedema; no evidence for appearance use.
note: Virilises female fetuses; masculinising side effects can be permanent.
currentQuick:
Danazol is an oral steroid prescribed for endometriosis, hereditary angioedema and some blood disorders. It has weak androgenic effects.
It has no studied role in appearance; mentions in muscle communities relate to its hormonal effects, not trials.
How it works: It suppresses LH and FSH, blocks several steroid-making enzymes and displaces hormones from SHBG, raising free testosterone. It also binds the androgen receptor.
Risks and caveats: Acne, hair growth, weight gain, lipid changes, liver enzyme elevation and permanent voice deepening are reported. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and prescription-only.
deepLead:
Danazol is an oral synthetic steroid derived from ethisterone. It has weak androgenic and anabolic activity, along with antigonadotropic, progestogenic and functional antioestrogenic effects. It is a prescription drug used mainly for endometriosis, with approved or off-label use in hereditary angioedema, fibrocystic breast disease and some blood disorders .
It was synthesised in 1963 at Sterling Winthrop and approved by the US FDA in the 1970s as the first drug specifically indicated for endometriosis; it has since been largely replaced for that purpose by GnRH analogues, which cause fewer masculinising effects . Its androgenic effects include acne, excess hair growth and irreversible voice deepening in women .
Danazol has no established role in appearance enhancement, and no studies of it for that purpose were found. Its blood-disorder uses, such as telomere diseases, are the subject of ongoing clinical research.

name: Tibolone (Livial)

angle.text: Tibolone is a menopause drug with weak androgenic activity, and some bodybuilding forum posters have discussed it as a mild anabolic. It is heavily trialled for menopause symptoms and bone; its use for looks is untested.

summary: A menopause drug with weak androgenic activity; heavily trialled for menopause, never for looks.
note: Not approved in the US; trials link it to stroke and breast cancer recurrence in specific groups.
currentQuick:
Tibolone is a prescription hormone therapy for menopause symptoms and osteoporosis in many countries, though not the US.
It has weak androgenic activity and is classed as an anabolic steroid in Canada, but no studies test it for appearance or muscle.
How it works: It is a prodrug whose metabolites act on estrogen, progesterone and androgen receptors in tissue-selective ways, and it lowers SHBG.
Risks and caveats: Trials and reviews report increased stroke risk in older women, higher breast cancer recurrence in survivors, and endometrial cancer and bleeding concerns. Acne and facial hair occur in some women.
deepLead:
Tibolone, sold as Livial and under other brand names, is an oral synthetic steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity, classed as a selective tissue estrogenic activity regulator (STEAR). It is prescribed to postmenopausal women for hot flushes, vaginal atrophy and prevention of osteoporosis .
It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in the Netherlands in 1988 and the UK in 1991. It is not approved in the United States, is a Canadian Schedule IV controlled substance because it is classed as an anabolic steroid, and is prohibited by WADA .
Large randomised trials and observational studies have examined its benefits and risks in menopausal women . No studies were found of tibolone for appearance or physique in men or women, though its androgenic activity and anabolic-steroid classification explain why it is mentioned in muscle-related contexts.

name: Gestrinone

angle.text: Gestrinone is an endometriosis steroid and the parent of the THG designer steroid, and has been mentioned in bodybuilding circles for its androgenic and antiestrogenic profile. Nothing has been studied for appearance.

summary: A weakly androgenic endometriosis steroid and the parent of the THG designer steroid; nothing studied for looks.
note: Banned in sport; androgenic effects such as voice deepening may be irreversible; not available in the US.
currentQuick:
Gestrinone is a prescription steroid used in some countries for endometriosis and sometimes fibroids. It acts on progesterone and androgen receptors and has weak anabolic activity.
It is discussed in performance circles because of that anabolic activity and because it is the chemical precursor of the designer steroid THG. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.
How it works: It binds the progesterone receptor strongly and the androgen receptor more weakly, suppresses the mid-cycle LH/FSH surge and ovarian steroid production, and lowers SHBG, which raises free testosterone.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include acne, oily skin, hair loss, hirsutism, weight gain and voice deepening, some of which may be irreversible, plus menstrual suppression. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, banned in sport, and not approved in the US.
deepLead:
Gestrinone is a synthetic steroid medication derived from 19-nortestosterone that combines progestogenic, antiprogestogenic, antiestrogenic and weak androgenic activity. It was introduced for medical use in 1986 and is marketed mainly for endometriosis, under brand names such as Dimetrose and Nemestran, in a limited number of countries; it is not available in the United States.
Its appearance-related profile in bodybuilding and performance-enhancement circles stems from its weak anabolic and androgenic properties, which led the International Olympic Committee to ban it in sport. Gestrinone is also the chemical precursor of tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), the designer steroid identified in 2003 in a doping case.
Published clinical research concerns gynecological conditions, chiefly endometriosis, and not muscle, body composition or other appearance outcomes. Reported adverse effects are largely androgenic, including acne, oily skin, hair loss, voice deepening and menstrual suppression.

name: Testolactone (Teslac)

angle.text: Testolactone is a discontinued steroidal aromatase inhibitor once used for breast cancer, and bodybuilders have discussed it for limiting estrogen during steroid use. It has been studied for cancer; nothing has been tested for looks.

summary: A discontinued first-generation steroidal aromatase inhibitor once used for breast cancer; nothing tested for looks.
note: Discontinued in 2008; superseded by later aromatase inhibitors.
currentQuick:
Testolactone (Teslac) was a prescription aromatase inhibitor approved in the US in 1970 for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It was discontinued in 2008.
It was also studied in children with precocious puberty and in infertile men. No trial has examined it for appearance.
How it works: It blocks the aromatase enzyme that converts androgens to estrogens, with lowering of estradiol that is modest compared with newer drugs.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include tingling, aches, hair loss, nausea and vomiting, with rarer allergic reactions and edema. It is no longer available for medical use.
deepLead:
Testolactone, sold as Teslac, is a steroidal first-generation aromatase inhibitor that was used as an anticancer drug for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It was first approved in the United States in 1970 and was discontinued in 2008.
Because aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, aromatase inhibitors have been of interest in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles for managing estrogen-related effects such as gynecomastia. Testolactone has been described as having been studied in men for infertility, gynecomastia and growth in children, but it is no longer available for medical use and is superseded by later agents.
No published trial has tested testolactone for appearance outcomes.

name: Formestane (Lentaron)

angle.text: Formestane is an injectable steroidal aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer, discussed in bodybuilding circles for controlling estrogen. It is studied only for cancer; nothing has been tested for appearance.

summary: An injectable steroidal aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer, now withdrawn; nothing tested for looks.
note: Never FDA-approved; European injectable withdrawn.
currentQuick:
Formestane (Lentaron) is an injectable steroidal aromatase inhibitor used for postmenopausal breast cancer. It is not orally active and the European product has been withdrawn.
It is mentioned in bodybuilding contexts as an estrogen suppressant, but no appearance trials exist.
How it works: It irreversibly binds aromatase and blocks estrogen synthesis; it also converts to 4-hydroxytestosterone, a weak androgen.
Risks and caveats: The available sources give little on side effects. It was not FDA-approved and the injectable has been withdrawn in Europe.
deepLead:
Formestane, sold as Lentaron, is a steroidal aromatase inhibitor that was given as an intramuscular depot injection to treat estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It is not orally active, was not approved by the US FDA, and the injectable form used in Europe has been withdrawn.
Wikipedia notes that it has also been used to suppress estrogen production arising from anabolic steroids or prohormones, which is the context in which it appears in bodybuilding discussion. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

name: Fadrozole

angle.text: Fadrozole is a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer in Japan and as a lab tool, and it is mentioned in bodybuilding circles as an estrogen blocker. Nothing has been tested for appearance.

summary: A nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer in Japan and as a lab tool; nothing tested for looks.
note: No appearance studies; sources give little on side effects.
currentQuick:
Fadrozole (Afema) is an oral aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer in Japan. Outside oncology it mainly appears in animal and lab research as a way to block estrogen production.
No human trial has examined it for appearance.
How it works: It reversibly binds the heme group of aromatase, reducing conversion of androgens to estrogens by about 80 to 90 percent at tested doses.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not detail its side effects. It is prescription-only and not approved in most countries.
deepLead:
Fadrozole (brand name Afema, Novartis) is a selective, nonsteroidal, oral aromatase inhibitor that is or has been used in Japan for breast cancer. It is classed as a Type II (reversible) inhibitor that binds the heme group of the aromatase enzyme.
Most published work on fadrozole beyond oncology is laboratory research in which it is used as a tool to block estrogen synthesis in fish, birds and rodents. No published human trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

name: Vorozole

angle.text: Vorozole is a discontinued third-generation aromatase inhibitor now used as a brain-imaging tracer, and it occasionally comes up as an estrogen blocker in physique forums. It has been studied for cancer; nothing has been tested for looks.

summary: A discontinued third-generation aromatase inhibitor now used as a brain-imaging tracer; nothing tested for looks.
note: Never marketed; sources give little on side effects.
currentQuick:
Vorozole is an oral aromatase inhibitor that was developed for cancer but dropped after trials showed no survival difference from megestrol acetate. It was never marketed.
Today it is mostly used as a PET tracer for studying aromatase in the brain. It has no studied appearance use.
How it works: It competitively blocks the aromatase enzyme, reducing estrogen synthesis.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not describe its adverse effects. It is an investigational compound without marketing approval.
deepLead:
Vorozole (developmental code R-76713, tentative brand name Rizivor) is a triazole-based, third-generation nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor that was investigated as an anticancer drug. Clinical development stopped after a comparison with megestrol acetate showed no difference in median survival, and anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane became the standard agents.
It is now best known in research as a radiotracer: carbon-11 labelled vorozole has been used with PET to map aromatase in the human brain. No published trial has tested vorozole for appearance outcomes.

name: Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren)

angle.text: Aminoglutethimide is an old adrenal-steroid and aromatase blocker that bodybuilders discussed for cutting cortisol and estrogen before contests. It has been studied for Cushing's syndrome and cancer; the physique use is untested.

summary: An old adrenal-steroid and aromatase blocker with a rough side-effect profile; cortisol-cutting for physique is untested.
note: Common lethargy; adrenal insufficiency risk; requires corticosteroid cover in medical use.
currentQuick:
Aminoglutethimide (Cytadren) began as an epilepsy drug and was later used to treat Cushing's syndrome and hormone-sensitive cancers by blocking steroid production.
Some bodybuilders have used it to cut cortisol and control estrogen. Wikipedia notes that this use has been questioned and that few users report positive experiences. No trials have tested it for appearance.
How it works: It inhibits several steroid-synthesis enzymes, notably P450scc in the adrenal gland and aromatase, lowering cortisol and estrogen.
Risks and caveats: Lethargy is the most common effect; rash, low blood pressure, liver toxicity and adrenal insufficiency are reported, and medical use pairs it with corticosteroid replacement. It is marketed in only a few countries.
deepLead:
Aminoglutethimide is an oral nonsteroidal glutarimide, sold under names including Cytadren, Elipten and Orimeten. It was introduced in 1960 as an anticonvulsant, then found to inhibit steroid synthesis, and was later used for Cushing's syndrome, postmenopausal breast cancer and prostate cancer. It was among the first adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors and the first aromatase inhibitor used clinically.
In bodybuilding, it has been used by some to lower cortisol and to curb estrogenic effects of anabolic steroids. Wikipedia notes that its usefulness for these purposes has been questioned, that few users report positive experiences and that risks are considered high. No published trial has tested it for appearance outcomes.

name: ATD (1,4,6-androstatrienedione)

angle.text: ATD was sold in prohormone-era supplements and is discussed in muscle-building circles as a way to limit estrogen conversion. Lab data support the mechanism; no human trials address look-related claims.

summary: A prohormone-era supplement aromatase inhibitor with lab data behind its mechanism and no human trials behind any look-related claim.
note: Banned in sport; can trigger a boldenone-positive drug test.
currentQuick:
ATD is a steroid-like supplement ingredient that was sold over the counter in the prohormone era, reportedly until around 2009. It is described as an aromatase inhibitor, which in theory lowers estrogen.
Its discussion in muscle-building communities centres on controlling estrogen. No human trial of its effects on muscle, gynecomastia or appearance was found.
How it works: Described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor: it binds the enzyme that makes estrogen from androgens and inactivates it. Evidence is from enzyme studies and an old monkey study.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. It is banned in sport and can reportedly cause a positive boldenone test. Products sold under varied names can be hard to identify.
deepLead:
ATD (1,4,6-androstatriene-3,17-dione) is a steroid-type compound described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor, meaning it binds the enzyme that converts androgens into estrogens and permanently inactivates it . It was sold in over-the-counter bodybuilding and prohormone-era supplements, reportedly until around 2009, and is discussed in muscle-building circles as a way to limit estrogen conversion .
Laboratory work has examined ATD-related structures as aromatase inhibitors in human placental enzyme preparations . No published human trial of ATD for body composition, gynecomastia or any other appearance outcome was identified. It is banned in sport as an aromatase inhibitor .

name: 6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione)

chain: Less gyno risk, leaner muscle look
angle.text: 6-OXO is used mainly by people on steroids or prohormones who say it limits estrogen rise and speeds recovery after cycles. One uncontrolled study showed hormone shifts without body-composition change.

summary: A prohormone-era aromatase inhibitor with an uncontrolled study showing hormone shifts and no body-composition change, and regulatory warnings.
note: FDA and Health Canada warnings; banned in sport.
currentQuick:
6-OXO is an oral supplement ingredient described as an irreversible aromatase inhibitor. Steroid and prohormone users have taken it to limit estrogen and gynecomastia.
The main human study was small, uncontrolled and partly industry-funded; it found hormone changes but no change in body composition.
How it works: Reported to permanently inactivate aromatase, lowering estradiol and raising LH and testosterone.
Risks and caveats: The FDA stated products containing it are adulterated, and Health Canada warned in 2008 of a blood-clotting risk. Acne is a listed possible effect. It is banned by WADA.
deepLead:
6-OXO (4-androstene-3,6,17-trione, also 4-AT) is an oral supplement ingredient described as a potent, irreversible aromatase inhibitor that may raise the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio . It has been used mainly by people using steroids or prohormones, who say it limits estrogen rise and gynecomastia risk, and after cycles to shorten recovery of testicular function .
The main human study is a 2007 eight-week trial in resistance-trained men that reported large rises in free testosterone and DHT but no change in body composition; it had no control group and was partly funded by commercial producers . The FDA and Health Canada have issued warnings about products containing it .

name: Damiana extract (Turnera diffusa)

angle.text: Damiana is a traditional aphrodisiac herb that some supplement users take as a natural anti-aromatase to support testosterone. A lab report found anti-aromatase constituents; human trials of the extract alone are absent.

summary: A traditional aphrodisiac herb with a lab report of anti-aromatase constituents and no human trials of the extract on its own.
note: Products may be mislabelled with a related species.
currentQuick:
Damiana is a shrub used in teas and liqueurs and sold as an herbal supplement. It is mentioned online as a natural aromatase inhibitor.
The basis is a 2008 laboratory study of its constituents; no human trial of damiana alone on estrogen or appearance was found.
How it works: Flavonoids such as pinocembrin and acacetin are reported to inhibit aromatase in lab assays.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are limited in the sources reviewed. Products may contain false damiana (Turnera ulmifolia), and combination products make effects hard to attribute.
deepLead:
Damiana (Turnera diffusa) is a small shrub native to southern Texas, Mexico, Central and South America and the Caribbean. It has been used in Mexican liqueurs, herbal teas and smoking blends, and in 19th-century patent medicines promoted as an aphrodisiac .
In bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles it is mentioned as a natural aromatase inhibitor. A 2008 paper in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology reported anti-aromatase activity of damiana constituents, and Wikipedia lists the flavonoids pinocembrin and acacetin as the compounds involved . These findings come from laboratory work; no human trial testing damiana for estrogen levels or appearance was identified.

name: White button mushroom extract

angle.text: White button mushroom extract is discussed as a food-derived aromatase inhibitor by users aiming for a better testosterone-to-estrogen balance. Evidence comes from lab assays, and human work is cancer-focused rather than about looks.

summary: A common food whose extracts inhibit aromatase in lab assays; human work is cancer-focused and not about looks.
note: Lab assay findings; no appearance outcomes tested in humans.
currentQuick:
White button mushroom is an everyday food. Extracts have been reported to inhibit aromatase in enzyme assays, which is why it appears in lists of natural aromatase inhibitors.
Human trials found were registered for cancer-related questions; none addressed appearance.
How it works: Compounds in the mushroom are reported to reduce aromatase enzyme activity in vitro.
Risks and caveats: As a common food it is widely eaten; safety data for concentrated extracts were not reviewed in depth. Wild lookalikes such as the death cap are dangerous, but that concerns foraging, not the cultivated product.
deepLead:
White button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus) is the common cultivated mushroom, grown in more than 70 countries; its brown form is sold as cremini and the mature form as portobello . Extracts of it are discussed as a food-derived aromatase inhibitor, meaning a substance that might reduce conversion of androgens to estrogens .
Wikipedia's aromatase inhibitor page reports that mushroom extracts inhibited aromatase in enzyme assays, with white mushroom showing the greatest effect, and cites a 2009 case-control study in southeast China linking higher mushroom intake to lower breast cancer incidence, which it describes as small and limited . Several small human trials have been registered; this article does not report results for them.

name: Afimoxifene (4-hydroxytamoxifen)

angle.text: Afimoxifene is the active form of tamoxifen, studied as a breast gel in women, and some men consider it for gynecomastia and a flatter chest. Published trials for male gynecomastia are absent.

summary: The active form of tamoxifen, studied as a breast gel in women; use for male gynecomastia has no published trials.
note: Investigational; trials were in women.
currentQuick:
Afimoxifene is the active metabolite of tamoxifen, formulated as a gel for application to the breast. It remains investigational.
Trials have been in women for breast pain, density and cancer settings. Its use for male gynecomastia, which is how it comes up in these communities, has not been tested in published trials found.
How it works: A SERM that blocks or mimics estrogen at estrogen receptors depending on the tissue; applied topically, the aim is local breast effects.
Risks and caveats: Not approved anywhere in the sources reviewed. Side-effect details for the gel were not reviewed in depth; the mastalgia trial was designed around avoiding the systemic effects of oral tamoxifen.
deepLead:
Afimoxifene, also called 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT), is an active metabolite of tamoxifen and a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM). It is an investigational drug, developed under the tentative brand name TamoGel as a topical gel for breast conditions .
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding contexts it is discussed as a topical option for gynecomastia. Published trials of the gel have been in women, for cyclical breast pain (mastalgia), breast density and breast cancer settings; no trial in men with gynecomastia was identified .

name: Raloxifene (Evista)

angle.text: Raloxifene is a prescription SERM for women's bone health that men use off-label to shrink gynecomastia. Forum posters report shrinkage and regrowth after stopping, while evidence for this use is limited.

summary: A prescription SERM approved for women's bone and breast risk, used off-label by men for gynecomastia on thin evidence.
note: Boxed warning: blood clots and stroke death; approved only for postmenopausal women.
currentQuick:
Raloxifene is a prescription SERM approved for osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction in postmenopausal women. Forum users discuss it as an off-label gynecomastia drug.
For that use, evidence is limited to a small retrospective review in adolescent boys.
How it works: It blocks estrogen action in breast tissue and mimics it in bone, depending on the tissue's receptor environment.
Risks and caveats: The label has a boxed warning for blood clots and stroke death; common effects include hot flashes, leg cramps and swelling. It is prescription-only and contraindicated in pregnancy.
deepLead:
Raloxifene (brand name Evista) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved in the US for treating and preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and for reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or at high risk . It acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast and uterine tissue .
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it is discussed as an off-label oral option for gynecomastia, including puberty-onset gynecomastia, often alongside or after tamoxifen . Published evidence for that use consists of small studies, for example a retrospective review in adolescent boys; it is not an approved indication .

name: Toremifene

angle.text: Toremifene is a tamoxifen-like SERM approved for breast cancer that men use off-label for gynecomastia and post-cycle recovery. Evidence for the appearance use is limited.

summary: A tamoxifen-like SERM approved for breast cancer and used off-label for gynecomastia; evidence for appearance use is thin and the label carries a QT warning.
note: Boxed warning for QT prolongation; prescription-only.
currentQuick:
Toremifene is a prescription SERM closely related to tamoxifen. It is approved for advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is mentioned as an estrogen blocker for gynecomastia. Reported benefit for gynecomastia comes from medical settings such as men on antiandrogen therapy, not from controlled studies of aesthetic use.
How it works: It binds estrogen receptors, blocking estrogen's effect in breast tissue while acting partly like estrogen in bone and some other tissues.
Risks and caveats: The US label carries a boxed warning for QT prolongation and arrhythmia, plus warnings on liver toxicity, uterine effects and pregnancy. Common effects include hot flashes, sweating and nausea. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Toremifene, sold mainly under the brand name Fareston, is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and a chlorinated analogue of tamoxifen. In the United States its only approved use is the treatment of metastatic breast cancer in postmenopausal women whose tumors are estrogen-receptor positive or of unknown status, and it is taken as a 60 mg oral tablet .
Outside that indication, toremifene appears in appearance- and muscle-related discussion because SERMs act as estrogen blockers in breast tissue. Medical literature describes reports of improvement in gynecomastia in men and prevention of bicalutamide-induced breast enlargement , and the drug is mentioned in bodybuilding and hormone-therapy contexts as an alternative to tamoxifen. These are off-label uses; the US label does not list them .
Large phase III trials found efficacy comparable to tamoxifen in advanced breast cancer . The US label carries a boxed warning for QT-interval prolongation, which can lead to the dangerous arrhythmia torsades de pointes . No controlled trial in healthy men using it for aesthetic or post-cycle purposes was found in the sources reviewed.

name: Fulvestrant (Faslodex)

angle.text: Fulvestrant is an injectable pure antiestrogen used for breast cancer, and it occasionally comes up in discussions of gynecomastia. No studies address appearance use.

summary: An injectable pure antiestrogen (SERD) used for breast cancer; no studies for appearance use.
note: Prescription oncology drug given by clinician-administered injection.
currentQuick:
Fulvestrant is a prescription injection that blocks and breaks down the estrogen receptor. It is approved for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
It is sometimes named in hormone-related discussions as a pure estrogen blocker, but published research covers cancer and rare pediatric conditions, not appearance goals.
How it works: It binds the estrogen receptor and marks it for destruction by the cell, reducing estrogen signaling.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include injection-site reactions, nausea, weakness, raised liver enzymes and clots. The label warns about bleeding risk, hepatic impairment and fetal harm. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Fulvestrant, sold as Faslodex and as generics, is an antiestrogen given by intramuscular injection. It is the first selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) approved for medical use and is used for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women .
It is a pure estrogen-receptor antagonist rather than a partial agonist like tamoxifen, which is why it is sometimes mentioned in muscle and hormone-related discussions as a 'pure' estrogen blocker. The sources reviewed describe only oncology and a few rare-disease uses; no study of fulvestrant for appearance goals was found.
Large randomized trials have tested it mainly in combination with CDK4/6 inhibitors and other targeted agents in advanced breast cancer . The US label lists injection-site reactions, bleeding risk, hepatic impairment and embryo-fetal toxicity among its warnings .

name: Bazedoxifene

angle.text: Bazedoxifene is a menopause and osteoporosis SERM, used for bone protection and hot flushes. It sits among estrogen-modulating drugs that men sometimes research, though no source ties it to looks.

summary: A menopause and osteoporosis SERM; nothing in the literature ties it to looks.
note: US product is a combination with conjugated estrogens and has a boxed warning.
currentQuick:
Bazedoxifene is a prescription SERM used for osteoporosis prevention and, with conjugated estrogens, for menopausal symptoms.
Published research concerns bone and menopause; no studies on appearance exist in the sources reviewed.
How it works: It binds estrogen receptors and acts like estrogen in bone while blocking estrogen in tissues such as the uterus, per preclinical work.
Risks and caveats: The combination product carries a boxed warning for endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disorders and probable dementia. Common effects include muscle spasms, nausea and diarrhea. It is prescription-only and contraindicated in pregnancy.
deepLead:
Bazedoxifene is a third-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) of the 2-phenylindole class, taken by mouth. It is used for the prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis and, combined with conjugated estrogens as Duavee or Duavive, for menopausal vasomotor symptoms .
It is not a hair, skin or muscle treatment, and the sources reviewed contain no appearance-related studies. It is included here because SERMs as a class are discussed in hormone and physique communities.
A 3-year randomized trial in women with osteoporosis found fewer new vertebral fractures than placebo . The combination product Duavee carries a boxed warning about endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disorders and probable dementia .
